title: Humbling oneself before God is not flattery
source_text: Εἶτα μὴ νοῶν, πῶς εἴρηται τὸ „πᾶς ὁ ὑψῶν ἑαυτὸν ταπεινωθήσεται,“ μηδὲ κἂν ἀπὸ τοῦ Πλάτωνος διδαχθεὶς ὅτι ὁ καλὸς καὶ ἀγαθὸς πορεύεται „ταπεινὸς καὶ κεκοσμημένος,“ μὴ εἰδὼς δὲ καὶ, ὥς φαμεν· „ταπεινώθητε οὖν ὑπὸ τὴν κραταιὰν χεῖρα τοῦ θεοῦ, ἵνα ὑμᾶς ὑψώσῃ ἐν καιρῷ,“ φησὶν ὅτι ἄνθρωποι μὲν ὀρθῶς δίκης προϊστάμενοι τοὺς ἐπὶ τοῖς ἀδικήμασιν ὀλοφυρομένους ἀποπαύουσι λόγων οἰκτρογόων, ἵνα μὴ πρὸς ἔλεον μᾶλλον ἢ πρὸς ἀλήθειαν δικασθῶσιν· ὁ θεὸς δ᾿ ἄρα οὐ πρὸς ἀλήθειαν ἀλλὰ πρὸς κολακείαν δικάζει. ποία γὰρ κολακεία, καὶ ποῖος λόγος οἰκτρόγοος κατὰ τὰς θείας γινόμενος γραφὰς, ἐπὰν ὁ ἁμαρτάνων λέγῃ ἐν ταῖς πρὸς θεὸν εὐχαῖς· „τὴν ἁμαρτίαν μου ἐγνώρισα, καὶ τὴν ἀνομίαν μου οὐκ ἐκάλυψα, εἶπα· ἐξαγορεύσω κατ᾿ ἐμοῦ τὴν ἀνομίαν μου τῷ κυρίῳ“ καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς; ἀλλὰ δύναται παραστῆσαι ὅτι οὐκ ἔστιν ἐπιστρεπτικὸν τὸ τοιοῦτον τῶν ἁμαρτανόντων, ὑπὸ τὸν θεὸν ἑαυτοὺς ταπεινούντων ἐν ταῖς εὐχαῖς; καὶ συγκεχυμένος δ᾿ ἀπὸ τῆς πρὸς τὸ κατηγορεῖν ὁρμῆς ἑαυτῷ ἐναντία λέγει, ὅπου μὲν ἐμφαίνων εἰδέναι ἀναμάρτητον ἄνθρωπον καὶ δίκαιον, μετ᾿ ἀρετῆς ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς πρὸς αὐτὸν ἄνω βλέποντα, ὅπου δ᾿ ἀποδεχόμενος τὸ λεγόμενον ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν, ὅτι „τίς ἄνθρωπος τελέως δίκαιος, ἢ τίς ἀναμάρτητος;“ ὡς ἀποδεχόμενος γὰρ αὐτό φησι· τοῦτο μὲν ἐπιεικῶς ἀληθὲς, ὅτι πέφυκέ πως τὸ ἀνθρώπινον φῦλον ἁμαρτάνειν· εἶτα ὡς μὴ πάντων καλουμένων ὑπὸ τοῦ λόγου φησίν· ἐχρῆν οὖν ἁπλῶς πάντας καλεῖν. εἴ γε πάντες ἁμαρτάνουσι, καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω δὲ παρεδείκνυμεν τὸν Ἰησοῦν εἰρηκέναι· „δεῦτε πάντες οἱ κοπιῶντες καὶ πεφορτισμένοι, κἀγὼ ἀναπαύσω ὑμᾶς.“ πάντες οὖν ἄνθρωποι διὰ τὴν τῆς ἁμαρτίας φύσιν „κοπιῶντες καὶ πεφορτισμένοι“ καλοῦνται ἐπὶ τὴν παρὰ τῷ λόγῳ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀνάπαυσιν· ἐξαπέστειλε γὰρ ὁ θεὸς „τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ καὶ ἰάσατο αὐτοὺς καὶ ἐῤῥύσατο αὐτοὺς ἐκ τῶν διαφθορῶν αὐτῶν.“
pass_a_gloss: Then not understanding (νοέω) how it is said, 'everyone who exalts (ὑψόω) himself will be humbled (ταπεινόω)', nor taught even by Plato that the fair and good man (καλὸς καὶ ἀγαθός) walks (πορεύομαι) 'humble and ordered' (ταπεινὸς καὶ κεκοσμημένος), not knowing either how we say: 'Be humbled therefore under the mighty (κραταιός) hand of God, that he may exalt you in season (ἐν καιρῷ)', he says that men rightly presiding over (προΐσταμαι) justice (δίκη) make those lamenting (ὀλοφύρομαι) over their crimes (ἀδίκημα) cease (ἀποπαύω) from piteous-wailing (οἰκτρόγοος) speeches, lest they be judged (δικάζω, pass.) toward pity (ἔλεος) rather than toward truth (ἀλήθεια); but God, then (ἄρα), judges not toward truth but toward flattery (κολακεία). For what flattery, and what piteous-wailing speech, comes about according to the divine Scriptures (θεῖαι γραφαί), when the sinner says in prayers (εὐχή) to God: 'My sin I made known (γνωρίζω), and my lawlessness (ἀνομία) I did not cover (καλύπτω); I said: I will declare out (ἐξαγορεύω) against myself my lawlessness to the Lord', and what follows? But can he establish (παρίστημι) that such a thing is not converting (ἐπιστρεπτικός) of sinners humbling themselves under God in prayers? And confused (συγχέω) from his impulse (ὁρμή) toward accusing (κατηγορέω) he says things contrary (ἐναντία) to himself: in one place indicating (ἐμφαίνω) that he knows a sinless and just man, with virtue from the beginning looking up to him; in another accepting (ἀποδέχομαι) what is said by us, 'What man is perfectly (τελέως) just, or who sinless?' For as accepting it he says: 'This indeed is reasonably (ἐπιεικῶς) true, that the human race (φῦλον) is somehow by nature (φύω, pf.) to sin.' Then, as though not all were called (καλέω) by the word (λόγος), he says: 'One ought then simply (ἁπλῶς) to call all, if indeed all sin.' And in what is above we showed Jesus to have said: 'Come, all who labour (κοπιάω) and are burdened (φορτίζω), and I will give you rest (ἀναπαύω).' All human beings then, because of the nature (φύσις) of sin labouring and burdened, are called to the rest (ἀνάπαυσις) with the Word of God; for God sent forth (ἐξαποστέλλω) 'his word and healed (ἰάομαι) them and rescued (ῥύομαι) them out of their corruptions (διαφθορά).'
pass_b_english: Then, not understanding the sense in which it is said, "Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled" (Luke 14:11; Luke 18:14), not having learned even from Plato that the noble and good man walks "humble and well ordered" (Plato, Laws 716a), and not knowing either that we say, "Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time" (1 Peter 5:6), he says that "men who rightly preside over justice stop those who lament over their crimes from making piteous, wailing speeches, so that they may not be judged by pity rather than by truth; but God, it seems, judges not by truth but by flattery."

Yet what flattery, what piteous and wailing speech, takes place according to the divine Scriptures when the sinner says in his prayers to God: "I made my sin known, and I did not hide my lawlessness; I said, I will confess my lawlessness against myself to the Lord" (Psalm 32:5), and the words that follow? Or can he show that such conduct on the part of sinners, when they humble themselves under God in their prayers, does not help to convert them?

Confused by his eagerness to accuse, he contradicts himself. In one place he implies that he knows a man who is without sin and just, who looks up to God with virtue from the beginning; in another he accepts what we say: "What man is perfectly just, or who is without sin?" For he speaks as one who accepts it: "This is fairly true, that the human race is somehow by nature inclined to sin." Then, as though not everyone were called by the word, he says: "So one ought simply to have called everyone, if indeed all sin."

Yet we showed earlier that Jesus said: "Come, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28). All human beings, then, "labouring and burdened" because of the nature of sin, are called to the rest that is found with the Word of God. For God sent forth "his Word, and healed them, and rescued them from their corruptions" (Psalm 107:20).

choices.choice: LXX renumbering: Psalm 31:5 LXX = Psalm 32:5 English; Psalm 106:20 LXX = Psalm 107:20 English. 'Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled' matches Luke 14:11 and Luke 18:14 word for word (Matthew 23:12 is worded differently); both Luke verses cited. Plato, Laws 716a: ταπεινὸς καὶ κεκοσμημένος, said of the man who follows Justice; Origen names Plato. 'Mighty hand of God' is 1 Peter 5:6 (Origen's text lacks the article before καιρῷ, as in standard texts). The saying Celsus reports, 'What man is perfectly just, or who is without sin?', matches no single verse; it may echo Ecclesiastes 7:20, Proverbs 20:9 or Job 15:14, but none is certain, so no inline citation. The TEI punctuates a full stop after πάντας καλεῖν; 'if indeed all sin' (εἴ γε πάντες ἁμαρτάνουσι) is taken as the end of Celsus's quoted sentence, since the following καὶ ... δέ begins Origen's answer. 'Called by the word' (ὑπὸ τοῦ λόγου) is left lowercase: it can mean the Christian message or the divine Word. In Psalm 107:20 'his Word' is capitalised because Origen reads it of the Word of God named in the same sentence; 'sent forth' stands outside the quotation marks because the edition marks the quotation from τὸν λόγον. Origen's Matthew 11:28 lacks πρός με ('to me'); translated as he quotes it. 'We showed earlier' points back to 2.73, where Origen quotes Matthew 11:28 in the same form (also without πρός με); 'labouring and burdened' is marked as a quotation in the edition and is put in quotation marks. The genitive τῶν ἁμαρτανόντων ... ταπεινούντων is read as the agents of τὸ τοιοῦτον ('such conduct on the part of sinners'), not as the object of ἐπιστρεπτικόν.
'so that their cases may not be decided' -> 'so that they may not be judged' (subject of δικασθῶσιν is the lamenters)
Rhetorical question on ἐπιστρεπτικόν recast: 'such conduct on the part of sinners ... does not help to convert them' (genitive is the agent, not the object)
Celsus's 'Then one ought simply' -> 'So one ought simply' (removes double 'Then'; οὖν)
'labouring and burdened' put in quotation marks as in the edition
Psalm 107:20: 'sent forth' moved outside the quotation, as the edition marks it (ἐξαπέστειλε)
Checked: Luke 14:11 / 18:14, Plato Laws 716a, 1 Peter 5:6, Psalm 31:5 LXX = 32:5, Matthew 11:28 (and back-reference 2.73 confirmed in source), Psalm 106:20 LXX = 107:20
